indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: 1. Building the Love and Culture of Reading
indicator.content_standard: B2.6.1.1: Read widely for pleasure and demonstrate independent reading and learning in the literary area
indicator.objective: Read a variety of age and level-appropriate books and texts from print and non-print

skills.description: Choose books that match their age, reading level, and interests from a provided collection.
Recognise and explore different types of texts (e.g., narratives, pop-up books, flip-the-page texts, and e-books if available).
Spend time reading independently for pleasure (with minimal support), demonstrating focus and enjoyment.
Talk about or share a book they have read (e.g., using the 'Author's Chair' strategy to show and tell).

misconceptions: Reading is only for schoolwork.
Only storybooks are real books.
You have to read the whole book in one sitting.
E-books are for playing games, not reading.
If a book has too many words, it's not for me.
Sharing a book means reading it out loud word-for-word.

questions.stem: Which book is best for a Basic 2 pupil who is just learning to read longer sentences?
options: A picture book with simple words
A long chapter book with no pictures
hints: Choose a book that matches the pupil's reading level.
Pictures and simple words help beginners.
questions.explanation: A picture book with simple words is age- and level-appropriate for a Basic 2 pupil.
questions.misconception: If a book has too many words, it's not for me.

questions.stem: Ama loves animals. Which book should she choose for reading time?
hints: Pick a book that matches her interest.
questions.explanation: A book about wild animals matches Ama's interest in animals.
questions.misconception: Only storybooks are real books.

questions.stem: Which of these is a 'just right' book for a Basic 2 pupil?
options: A book with a few sentences per page and pictures
A book with 100 pages and no pictures
A book with very small print
hints: A 'just right' book is not too hard and not too easy.
It should match the pupil's reading level.
questions.explanation: A book with a few sentences per page and pictures is suitable for a Basic 2 pupil.
questions.misconception: If a book has too many words, it's not for me.

questions.stem: Which book would you choose if you want to read for fun?
hints: Choose a book that is entertaining.
questions.explanation: A storybook about Ananse is a fun book to read for pleasure.
questions.misconception: Reading is only for schoolwork.

questions.stem: What is a pop-up book?
options: A book with pictures that stand up when you open the page
A book you read on a phone
hints: It has parts that pop up.
It is fun to look at.
questions.explanation: A pop-up book has pictures that stand up when the page is opened.
questions.misconception: Only storybooks are real books.

questions.stem: What is an e-book?
options: A book you read on a computer or tablet
hints: You read it on a screen.
questions.explanation: An e-book is an electronic book read on a device like a tablet or computer.
questions.misconception: E-books are for playing games, not reading.

questions.stem: Which of these is a print book?
hints: Print books are made of paper.
questions.explanation: A storybook you can hold is a print book.
questions.misconception: E-books are for playing games, not reading.

questions.stem: Which of these is a flip-the-page book?
options: A book with pages you lift to see hidden pictures
A book you read on a phone
hints: You flip parts of the page.
questions.explanation: A flip-the-page book has flaps you lift to reveal pictures or words.
questions.misconception: Only storybooks are real books.

questions.stem: What should you do if you want to share a book you read with the class?
options: Tell them the title and what it is about
hints: You don't have to read every word.
questions.explanation: Sharing a book means telling others the title and what it is about.
questions.misconception: Sharing a book means reading it out loud word-for-word.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B2.5.10.1: Use phonics knowledge to spell words
indicator.objective: Use phonics knowledge to spell words with irregular phonetic letter pattern

skills.description: Identify words that do not follow standard phonetic spelling rules (e.g., the, said, was, you, have, face).
Spell phonetically irregular words correctly from memory, dictation, or a word bank.
Fill in the blanks in sentences or write oral/written sentences using the correctly spelled irregular words.

misconceptions: All words can be sounded out letter by letter.
Irregular words are impossible to learn.
If it sounds right, it is spelled right.
Irregular words don't need to be used in sentences.
You only need to spell them orally.
Long words are always irregular, and short words are always regular.

questions.stem: Which word is a phonetically irregular word?
hints: It is a very common word.
It does not sound like its letters.
questions.explanation: The word 'the' is irregular because the 'e' is not pronounced as expected.
questions.misconception: All words can be sounded out letter by letter.

questions.stem: Which word is an irregular word you must learn by sight?
hints: It sounds like 'sed' but is spelled differently.
questions.explanation: Said is irregular because it does not sound like it is spelled.
questions.misconception: If it sounds right, it is spelled right.

questions.stem: Which of these words is irregular?
hints: The 'a' is not pronounced as expected.
questions.explanation: Have is irregular because the 'a' sounds like a short 'a' but is not spelled with 'a'.
questions.misconception: All words can be sounded out letter by letter.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled irregularly?
questions.explanation: You is irregular because the 'ou' sounds like 'oo'.
questions.misconception: Long words are always irregular, and short words are always regular.

questions.stem: Which spelling is correct?
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'the'.
questions.misconception: If it sounds right, it is spelled right.

questions.stem: Which spelling is correct?
hints: It is a past tense of 'say'.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'said'.
questions.misconception: If it sounds right, it is spelled right.

questions.stem: Which spelling is correct?
hints: It is a past tense of 'is'.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'was'.
questions.misconception: If it sounds right, it is spelled right.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'This is ___ book.'
hints: It is a common irregular word.
questions.explanation: The correct word is 'my'.
questions.misconception: Irregular words don't need to be used in sentences.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The boy ___ his name was Kofi.'
hints: It is a past tense of 'say'.
questions.explanation: The correct word is 'said'.
questions.misconception: If it sounds right, it is spelled right.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B2.5.9.1: Understand simple sentences in writing
indicator.objective: Identify nouns and verbs in simple sentences

skills.description: Recognise and name nouns (naming words for people, places, things) in a simple sentence.
Recognise and name verbs (doing words/action words) in a simple sentence.
Match a noun to a suitable verb to form a meaningful simple sentence.

misconceptions: Verbs are only physical actions.
Nouns are only objects.
Every word after the first is a verb.
A word can only be a noun or a verb.
Nouns and verbs are the same thing.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'The boy runs' is a noun (naming word)?
hints: It is not an action word.
questions.explanation: Boy is a noun because it names a person.
questions.misconception: Nouns are only objects.

questions.stem: Which of these is a noun?
hints: It is a thing you can sit on.
It is not an action word.
questions.explanation: Chair is a noun because it names a thing.
questions.misconception: Nouns are only objects.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'Ama sings a song', which word is a noun?
hints: It is a name of a person.
questions.explanation: Ama is a noun because it names a person. 'Song' is also a noun.
questions.misconception: Every word after the first is a verb.

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is a noun? 'The children play in the park.'
questions.explanation: Children is a noun. 'Park' is also a noun.
questions.misconception: Every word after the first is a verb.

questions.stem: Which of these is a noun?
hints: It is not an action or describing word.
questions.explanation: School is a noun because it names a place.
questions.misconception: Nouns are only objects.

questions.stem: Which word in 'The cat sleeps' is a verb?
hints: It tells what the cat does.
questions.explanation: Sleeps is the verb because it tells what the cat does.
questions.misconception: Verbs are only physical actions.

questions.stem: Which of these is a verb (doing word)?
hints: You do it with your legs.
questions.explanation: Run is a verb because it is an action.
questions.misconception: Verbs are only physical actions.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The bird flies', which word is the verb?
hints: It tells what the bird does.
questions.explanation: Flies is the verb because it tells what the bird does.
questions.misconception: Verbs are only physical actions.

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is a verb? 'The teacher writes on the board.'
hints: It tells what the teacher does.
questions.explanation: Writes is the verb because it tells what the teacher does.
questions.misconception: Every word after the first is a verb.

questions.stem: Which of these sentences has a verb that is NOT an action you can see?
hints: The verb 'is' is not an action.
Look for a state of being.
questions.explanation: The verb 'is' is not an action you can see; it is a state-of-being verb.
questions.misconception: Verbs are only physical actions.

questions.stem: Which verb matches the noun 'dog'?
hints: What sound does a dog make?
Choose the verb that makes sense.
questions.explanation: Barks matches the noun 'dog' because dogs bark.
questions.misconception: Nouns and verbs are the same thing.

questions.stem: Which verb matches the noun 'bird'?
hints: What does a bird do in the sky?
Choose the verb that makes sense.
questions.explanation: Flies matches the noun 'bird' because birds fly.
questions.misconception: Nouns and verbs are the same thing.

questions.stem: Which verb matches the noun 'teacher'?
hints: Choose the verb that makes sense.
questions.explanation: Teaches matches the noun 'teacher'.
questions.misconception: Nouns and verbs are the same thing.

questions.stem: Which pair of noun and verb makes a meaningful sentence?
options: The boy swims in the sky.
hints: Choose the pair that makes sense in real life.
questions.explanation: The boy runs.' is a meaningful sentence because boys can run.
questions.misconception: A word can only be a noun or a verb.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B2.5.9.1: Understand simple sentences in writing
indicator.objective: Identify the structure of simple sentences

skills.description: Recognise the basic Subject + Verb (Name + Doing word) structure of a simple sentence.
Identify the naming part (subject) and the doing part (verb) in a simple sentence.
Distinguish a complete simple sentence from a fragment.

misconceptions: A sentence is just any group of words.
The subject is always at the beginning.
A sentence needs many words to be complete.
The doing word is always an action you can see.
Any word that describes a noun is a verb.

questions.stem: Which of these is a simple sentence with a subject and a verb?
hints: A sentence needs a naming part and a doing part.
Look for both a person and an action.
questions.explanation: Yaa came.' has a subject (Yaa) and a verb (came).
questions.misconception: A sentence is just any group of words.

questions.stem: Which sentence follows the pattern 'Subject + Verb'?
questions.explanation: Musa ate.' follows the Subject + Verb pattern.
questions.misconception: A sentence is just any group of words.

questions.stem: Which of these is a complete simple sentence?
hints: A sentence needs both a subject and a verb.
questions.explanation: The dog barked.' is a complete simple sentence with a subject and a verb.
questions.misconception: A sentence needs many words to be complete.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The girl danced', what is the doing word (verb)?
hints: It tells what the girl did.
questions.explanation: Danced is the doing word (verb) because it tells what the girl did.
questions.misconception: The doing word is always an action you can see.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'Ofori laughed', what is the naming part (subject)?
hints: It is the person in the sentence.
questions.explanation: Ofori is the naming part (subject) because it names the person doing the action.
questions.misconception: The doing word is always an action you can see.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence 'The cat sleeps' is the verb?
hints: It tells what the cat does.
questions.explanation: Sleeps is the verb because it tells what the cat does.
questions.misconception: The doing word is always an action you can see.

questions.stem: Which of these is a complete sentence?
hints: A complete sentence needs a subject and a verb.
Look for both a person and an action.
questions.explanation: The boy ran.' is complete because it has a subject and a verb.
questions.misconception: A sentence is just any group of words.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a complete sentence?
options: The girl with the red bag.
hints: A sentence needs a verb (doing word).
Look for the option without an action.
questions.explanation: The girl with the red bag.' is not a complete sentence because it has no verb.
questions.misconception: A sentence needs many words to be complete.

questions.stem: Which of these is a complete sentence?
hints: Look for a subject and a verb.
Only one option has an action word.
questions.explanation: Ama reads.' is complete because it has a subject (Ama) and a verb (reads).
questions.misconception: A sentence is just any group of words.

questions.stem: Why is 'The big house' not a complete sentence?
hints: A sentence needs a doing word.
The house is not doing anything.
questions.explanation: The big house' is not a complete sentence because it has no verb (doing word).
questions.misconception: A sentence needs many words to be complete.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The baby cried loudly', what is the verb?
hints: It tells what the baby did.
questions.explanation: Cried is the verb because it tells what the baby did.
questions.misconception: Any word that describes a noun is a verb.

questions.stem: Which of these is a complete sentence?
options: The tall boy in the blue shirt ran home.
The tall boy in the blue shirt.
hints: A complete sentence needs both a subject and a verb.
Look for the sentence with an action.
questions.explanation: The tall boy in the blue shirt ran home.' is complete because it has a subject and a verb (ran).
questions.misconception: A sentence needs many words to be complete.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B2.5.7.1: Understand and identify the use of prepositions
indicator.objective: Use prepositions to form simple sentences to indicate position and time

skills.description: Use prepositions correctly in sentences to show position.
Use prepositions correctly in sentences to show time.
Construct simple, grammatically correct sentences using prepositions to describe position or time.

misconceptions: You can leave out the preposition if the meaning is clear.
Prepositions are optional in simple sentences.
You can use 'in' and 'on' interchangeably for time.
Prepositions are always followed by a noun or pronoun.
One sentence can only have one preposition.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'The bag is ___ the table.'
hints: It shows where the bag is.
The bag is resting on top.
questions.explanation: On shows that the bag is on top of the table.
questions.misconception: Prepositions are optional in simple sentences.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'Esi sat ___ a chair ___ the room.'
questions.explanation: Esi sat on a chair in the room.
questions.misconception: You can leave out the preposition if the meaning is clear.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the preposition correctly to show position?
options: The cat is under the table.
The cat is under on the table.
The cat is under at the table.
The cat is under for the table.
hints: The other options use two prepositions incorrectly.
questions.explanation: The cat is under the table.' uses 'under' correctly to show position.
questions.misconception: One sentence can only have one preposition.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'We go to school ___ Monday.'
hints: It is used with days of the week.
questions.explanation: On is used with days of the week.
questions.misconception: You can use 'in' and 'on' interchangeably for time.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'The teacher went to the classroom ___ night.'
questions.explanation: At is used with 'night'.
questions.misconception: You can use 'in' and 'on' interchangeably for time.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the preposition correctly for time?
options: I have a test on 1st May.
I have a test in 1st May.
I have a test at 1st May.
I have a test by 1st May.
questions.explanation: On is used with specific dates.
questions.misconception: You can use 'in' and 'on' interchangeably for time.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'in' correctly for time?
options: I wake up in the morning.
hints: Not with days or specific times.
questions.explanation: In is used with 'the morning'.
questions.misconception: You can use 'in' and 'on' interchangeably for time.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a preposition correctly to show position?
options: The shoes are under the bed.
The shoes are under on the bed.
The shoes are under at the bed.
The shoes are under for the bed.
questions.explanation: The shoes are under the bed.' uses 'under' correctly.
questions.misconception: One sentence can only have one preposition.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B2.5.7.1: Understand and identify the use of prepositions
indicator.objective: Identify prepositions in sentences to indicate days, dates and places

skills.description: Recognise prepositions that show place or location in a sentence (e.g., in, on, at, under).
Recognise prepositions that show days, dates, or time (e.g., on Monday, on 1st May, at night, in the morning).
Distinguish prepositions from other words (nouns, verbs, adjectives) in a sentence.

misconceptions: Prepositions are only for places.
Every small word is a preposition.
You can use any preposition with any day or date.
Prepositions must come at the end of a sentence.
The preposition 'on' is only for physical surfaces.

questions.stem: Which word in the sentence 'The cat is on the mat' shows place?
hints: It tells where the cat is.
questions.explanation: The word 'on' shows the place where the cat is.
questions.misconception: Prepositions are only for places.

questions.stem: Which word is a preposition showing place?
questions.explanation: Under is a preposition that shows place.
questions.misconception: Every small word is a preposition.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'The pencil is ___ the bag.'
questions.explanation: In shows that the pencil is inside the bag.
questions.misconception: The preposition 'on' is only for physical surfaces.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a preposition to show place?
options: The boy is in the room.
hints: Look for a word that shows where.
The other sentences describe or tell actions.
questions.explanation: In shows the place where the boy is.
questions.misconception: Prepositions are only for places.

questions.stem: Which word in 'I saw a bird on Monday' shows a day?
questions.explanation: On shows the day when the bird was seen.
questions.misconception: The preposition 'on' is only for physical surfaces.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'I have a test ___ 1st May.'
hints: We use this preposition with dates.
It is the same word used with days.
questions.explanation: On is used with specific dates like '1st May'.
questions.misconception: You can use any preposition with any day or date.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'at' correctly for time?
options: The teacher went to the classroom at night.
The teacher went to the classroom at Monday.
The teacher went to the classroom at May.
The teacher went to the classroom at morning.
questions.explanation: At is used with 'night'.
questions.misconception: You can use any preposition with any day or date.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a preposition to show time?
hints: Look for a word that shows when.
questions.explanation: At night shows the time when they are playing.
questions.misconception: Prepositions are only for places.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the correct preposition for time?
hints: We use 'on' with days of the week.
The other options are not standard for days.
questions.explanation: On is the correct preposition to use with days of the week.
questions.misconception: You can use any preposition with any day or date.

questions.stem: Which word is a preposition?
hints: It is not an adjective or verb.
questions.explanation: In is a preposition.
questions.misconception: Every small word is a preposition.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The boy is in the room', which word is a preposition?
hints: It shows where the boy is.
It is not a noun or article.
questions.explanation: In is the preposition showing place.
questions.misconception: Every small word is a preposition.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a preposition?
questions.explanation: Happy is an adjective, not a preposition.
questions.misconception: Every small word is a preposition.

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is a preposition? 'She went to the market on Monday.'
questions.explanation: To is a preposition showing direction.
questions.misconception: Every small word is a preposition.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a preposition to show a day?
options: We have football in the field.
We have football under the tree.
hints: Look for the day of the week.
questions.explanation: On Tuesday uses 'on' to show a day.
questions.misconception: Prepositions are only for places.

questions.stem: How many prepositions are in this sentence: 'The boy is in the room on Monday.'
hints: One shows place, one shows time.
questions.explanation: There are two prepositions: 'in' (place) and 'on' (time).
questions.misconception: Prepositions are only for places.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B2.5.5.1: Apply knowledge of adjectives in communication
indicator.objective: Identify and use simple sentences to describe the weather and show quantity and position or order of people and things.

skills.description: Recognise and use adjectives to describe weather conditions (e.g., cold, hot, sunny, rainy, windy) in simple sentences.
Recognise and use words that show quantity (e.g., numbers, 'many', 'few', 'some') in simple sentences.
Recognise and use words that show position or order (e.g., first, second, last, on, in, under) in simple sentences.
Write simple, grammatically correct sentences combining weather, quantity or position/order adjectives correctly.

misconceptions: Weather words are nouns, not adjectives.
Quantity words don't need to match the noun.
Position words are the same as quantity words.
Adjectives always come before the noun in the exact same way.
Any describing word is an adjective.
Weather is always described with 'is'.

questions.stem: Which word describes the weather when the sun is shining brightly?
questions.explanation: Sunny describes weather with bright sunshine.
questions.misconception: Weather words are nouns, not adjectives.

questions.stem: Which word describes the weather when it is very cold?
hints: It is the opposite of hot.
questions.explanation: Cold describes low temperature weather.
questions.misconception: Weather words are nouns, not adjectives.

questions.stem: Choose the correct describing word: 'It is ______ today, so I will carry an umbrella.'
hints: An umbrella is used in this weather.
questions.explanation: Rainy weather means it is raining, so an umbrella is needed.
questions.misconception: Weather is always described with 'is'.

questions.stem: Which word shows quantity in 'I have two pencils'?
questions.explanation: Two shows the quantity of pencils.
questions.misconception: Quantity words don't need to match the noun.

questions.stem: Which word shows quantity?
hints: It tells how much or how many.
It is not an object or action.
questions.explanation: Many shows quantity.
questions.misconception: Quantity words don't need to match the noun.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'There are ______ children in the class.'
hints: Use a word that means 'a lot'.
questions.explanation: Many is used with countable nouns like children.
questions.misconception: Quantity words don't need to match the noun.

questions.stem: Which word shows position in 'The book is on the table'?
hints: It tells where the book is.
questions.explanation: On shows the position of the book.
questions.misconception: Position words are the same as quantity words.

questions.stem: Which word shows order?
hints: It tells the order of things.
questions.explanation: First shows order.
questions.misconception: Position words are the same as quantity words.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The cat is ______ the table.'
hints: It tells where the cat is.
questions.explanation: Under shows the position of the cat.
questions.misconception: Position words are the same as quantity words.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B2.5.4.1: Apply knowledge of action words in communication
indicator.objective: Use the simple present tense to express habitual actions (simple truths, interest, feelings and opinions)

skills.description: Use the simple present tense to describe daily routines and habits.
Use the simple present tense to state facts or general truths.
Use the simple present tense to talk about likes, interests, and feelings.
Use the simple present tense to share opinions or beliefs.

misconceptions: Present tense is only for things happening right now.
Every verb in the present tense needs an '-s'.
Feelings and opinions are the same as facts.
Action words are only things you can see people doing.
Habits are just things you do once.

questions.stem: Which sentence tells about something you do every day?
options: I brush my teeth every morning.
I am brushing my teeth now.
I will brush my teeth tomorrow.
hints: Look for a sentence about a daily routine.
The simple present tense is used for habits.
questions.explanation: I brush my teeth every morning.' tells about a daily habit, so it uses the simple present tense.
questions.misconception: Present tense is only for things happening right now.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the simple present tense for a habit?
options: She reads a book every night.
She is reading a book now.
hints: Look for the sentence with 'every night'.
questions.explanation: She reads a book every night.' describes a habit, so it uses the simple present tense.
questions.misconception: Present tense is only for things happening right now.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'Kofi ___ football every Saturday.'
hints: Kofi is one person, so the verb needs '-s'.
questions.explanation: Kofi is singular, so the correct simple present form is 'plays'.
questions.misconception: Every verb in the present tense needs an '-s'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is about a daily routine?
options: I eat breakfast at 7 o'clock every day.
questions.explanation: I eat breakfast at 7 o'clock every day.' describes a routine, so it uses the simple present tense.
questions.misconception: Habits are just things you do once.

questions.stem: Which sentence tells a simple truth?
options: I am going to school now.
hints: A simple truth is always true.
It does not change from moment to moment.
questions.explanation: The sun is hot.' is a simple truth because it states a fact that is generally true.
questions.misconception: Present tense is only for things happening right now.

questions.stem: Which sentence states a simple truth?
hints: A simple truth is a fact about the world.
questions.explanation: Lemons are sour.' is a simple truth because it states a general fact.
questions.misconception: Feelings and opinions are the same as facts.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the simple present for a fact?
hints: It does not depend on the time.
questions.explanation: Water boils at 100 degrees.' states a scientific fact using the simple present tense.
questions.misconception: Present tense is only for things happening right now.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a simple truth, NOT a habit or an opinion?
hints: A simple truth is a fact about the world.
It is not about what someone does or thinks.
questions.explanation: The earth is round.' is a simple truth. The others are a habit, an opinion, and an interest.
questions.misconception: Feelings and opinions are the same as facts.

questions.stem: Which sentence tells about a feeling?
hints: A feeling tells how someone feels inside.
questions.explanation: I am happy.' tells about a feeling.
questions.misconception: Feelings and opinions are the same as facts.

questions.stem: Which sentence expresses an interest?
hints: An interest tells what you enjoy.
questions.explanation: I like playing football.' expresses an interest.
questions.misconception: Feelings and opinions are the same as facts.

questions.stem: Which sentence expresses a feeling in the simple present tense?
hints: A feeling word tells how someone feels.
questions.explanation: She is excited.' expresses a feeling using the simple present tense.
questions.misconception: Present tense is only for things happening right now.

questions.stem: Which sentence shares an opinion?
options: I think rice is better than tofu.
hints: An opinion tells what someone thinks or believes.
questions.explanation: I think rice is better than tofu.' shares an opinion.

You can use capital letters anywhere for emphasis.

questions.stem: Which sentence has the first word correctly capitalised?

Other words are lowercase unless proper nouns.

questions.stem: Which word is a proper noun and needs a capital letter?

questions.stem: Which lowercase letter matches the uppercase letter 'A'?

questions.stem: Which uppercase letter matches the lowercase letter 'g'?

questions.stem: Which word is copied correctly? The word is 'book'.
questions.explanation: The correct copy of 'book' is 'book' with all lowercase letters.
questions.misconception: Every letter in a word must be capitalised.

questions.stem: Which copy has correct spacing? The original is 'The cat is fat.'
hints: Words should have one space between them.
questions.explanation: The correct spacing is 'The cat is fat.' with one space between each word.

questions.stem: Which word has correct spacing?

questions.misconception: Spacing between letters is the same as spacing between words.

indicator.subject: English Language

indicator.objective: Copy sentences clearly

Copy a sentence from the board or a book without missing or adding words.

questions.misconception: If I read a word wrong, I should just keep going.

questions.misconception: If I read a word wrong, I should just keep going.

questions.misconception: Context only helps with big words.

questions.misconception: Context only helps with big words.

questions.misconception: Accuracy means reading every single word perfectly on the first try.

questions.misconception: Accuracy means reading every single word perfectly on the first try.

questions.explanation: Ama gave the dog her bread because the dog was hungry.

questions.stem: Read: 'The boy forgot his umbrella. He got wet in the rain.' What caused the boy to get wet?
hints: It is used to keep off rain.
questions.explanation: The boy got wet because he forgot his umbrella.
questions.misconception: Characters are separate from events.

questions.stem: Read: 'The teacher praised Ama because she helped a friend.' Why did the teacher praise Ama?
questions.explanation: The teacher praised Ama because she helped a friend.
questions.misconception: Only the main character matters.

questions.stem: Read: 'The old woman smiled when the children helped her cross the road.' How did the event affect the old woman?
hints: What did she do? She smiled.
questions.explanation: The old woman smiled, showing that the event made her happy.
questions.misconception: Only the main character matters.

questions.stem: Read: 'The boy planted a seed. He watered it every day. In the end, he had a beautiful flower.' How are the beginning and the end connected?
options: The seed he planted grew into a flower
The boy forgot about the seed
The flower was there from the start
hints: What did he plant at the beginning?
What did he have at the end?
questions.explanation: The seed planted at the beginning grew into the flower at the end.
questions.misconception: The ending has nothing to do with the beginning.

questions.stem: Read: 'The sky was dark. The wind blew strongly. Then, the rain fell.' How are the ideas connected?
options: Dark sky and strong wind are signs of rain
The rain caused the dark sky
hints: Dark sky and wind lead to rain.
questions.explanation: The dark sky and strong wind are connected to the rain because they are signs that rain is coming.
questions.misconception: Ideas in a text are unconnected.

questions.stem: Read: 'The boy forgot his homework. He was worried. He told the teacher.' Why was the boy worried?
questions.explanation: The boy was worried because he forgot his homework.
questions.misconception: Ideas in a text are unconnected.

questions.stem: Read: 'The children cleaned the classroom. The teacher was happy. She gave them a reward.' How are the children's actions and the reward connected?
options: They were rewarded for being noisy
They were rewarded for being late
hints: The teacher was happy because of it.
questions.explanation: The children were rewarded because they cleaned the classroom, which made the teacher happy.
questions.misconception: Ideas in a text are unconnected.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama helped her mother wash the dishes.' Have you ever helped your mother at home?
options: Yes, I have helped my mother
No, I have never helped my mother
questions.explanation: Many children help their parents at home, just like Ama.
questions.misconception: A text has nothing to do with my life.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi lost his pencil and was very sad.' Have you ever lost something and felt sad?
hints: Think about a time you lost something.
questions.explanation: Many people feel sad when they lose something, just like Kofi.
questions.misconception: A text has nothing to do with my life.

questions.stem: Read: 'The boy felt nervous before his first day at a new school.' How might you feel on your first day at a new school?
hints: How do you feel when you try something new?
questions.explanation: It is normal to feel nervous on your first day at a new school, just like the boy in the story.
questions.misconception: A text has nothing to do with my life.

questions.stem: Read: 'The girl was excited to visit her grandmother.' Who do you like to visit?
hints: Think about a family member you enjoy seeing.
questions.explanation: Visiting relatives, like a grandmother, is a common experience that brings excitement.
questions.misconception: A text has nothing to do with my life.

questions.stem: Read: 'The boy was proud when he finished his homework on time.' What makes you feel proud?
hints: Proud is a feeling of achievement.
It happens when you do something good.
questions.explanation: You feel proud when you achieve something, like finishing homework on time.
questions.misconception: A text has nothing to do with my life.

questions.stem: Read: 'The sun was hot. The children were thirsty. They drank water.' How are these ideas connected?
options: The hot sun made them thirsty
They drank water because they were tired
questions.explanation: The hot sun made the children thirsty, which is why they drank water.
questions.misconception: Ideas in a text are unconnected.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B2.2.7.2: Use knowledge skills and techniques of reading to understand and interpret texts
indicator.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of information texts

skills.description: Recognise an information text (a text that gives facts about a topic) and distinguish it from a story.
State the purpose of an information text (e.g., to inform, to teach, to explain).
Identify features of information texts (e.g., title, headings, facts, diagrams, labels).

misconceptions: All texts are stories.
Information texts are only for adults.
Headings are just decoration.
An information text must have pictures.
The purpose is always to entertain.

questions.stem: Which of these is a text that gives facts about a topic?
hints: It is not a made-up story.
questions.explanation: An information text gives facts about a topic.
questions.misconception: All texts are stories.

questions.stem: Read this: 'Cows eat grass. They give us milk.' What kind of text is this?
hints: It does not have characters or a plot.
questions.explanation: This is an information text because it gives facts about cows.
questions.misconception: All texts are stories.

questions.stem: Which of these sentences would you find in an information text about malaria?
options: The mosquito flew to the moon.
hints: The other sentences are made up.
questions.explanation: Malaria is spread by mosquitoes' is a fact, so it belongs in an information text.
questions.misconception: All texts are stories.

questions.stem: How is an information text different from a story?
options: An information text gives facts, while a story tells about made-up events.
An information text is always longer.
An information text has more characters.
hints: One is true, the other is made up.
Think about what you learn from each.
questions.explanation: An information text gives facts, while a story tells about events that may be made up.
questions.misconception: All texts are stories.

questions.stem: A text says: 'Once upon a time, a tortoise tricked a lion.' What type of text is this?
hints: It starts with 'Once upon a time'.
It has characters like a tortoise and a lion.
questions.explanation: This is a story because it starts with 'Once upon a time' and tells about made-up events.
questions.misconception: All texts are stories.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of an information text?
hints: Think about what you learn from it.
questions.explanation: The purpose of an information text is to give facts and teach the reader.
questions.misconception: The purpose is always to entertain.

questions.stem: Why do we read information texts?
hints: What can you learn from facts?
It helps you know more about a topic.
questions.explanation: We read information texts to learn new facts about the world.
questions.misconception: The purpose is always to entertain.

questions.stem: A text titled 'How to Wash Your Hands' is written to:
options: Teach you how to do something
questions.explanation: This information text is written to teach you the steps for washing your hands.
questions.misconception: The purpose is always to entertain.

questions.stem: A text gives facts about how to prevent malaria. What is its purpose?
options: To inform people about malaria prevention
To tell a story about a mosquito
hints: The text is about preventing a disease.
questions.explanation: The purpose is to inform people about how to prevent malaria.
questions.misconception: The purpose is always to entertain.

questions.stem: An information text about 'The Importance of Exercise' is written to:
options: Explain why exercise is good for you
hints: The word 'importance' means why it matters.
questions.explanation: The purpose is to explain why exercise is important for your health.
questions.misconception: The purpose is always to entertain.

questions.stem: Which of these is a feature of an information text?
hints: It is like a title for a section.
questions.explanation: Headings are a feature of information texts used to organise information.
questions.misconception: Headings are just decoration.

questions.stem: What is usually at the top of an information text to tell you the topic?
hints: It tells you what the text is about.
It is the first thing you see.
questions.explanation: A title at the top tells you the topic of an information text.
questions.misconception: Headings are just decoration.

questions.stem: Information texts often include diagrams. What is a diagram?
hints: It is a picture with labels.
questions.explanation: A diagram is a drawing that shows information, often with labels.
questions.misconception: An information text must have pictures.

questions.stem: Which feature would help you find a specific fact quickly in an information text?
hints: It groups information under a title.
It helps you jump to the right section.
questions.explanation: A heading groups information under a title, helping you find facts quickly.
questions.misconception: Headings are just decoration.

questions.stem: An information text about 'The Parts of a Plant' has labels pointing to roots, stem, leaves, and flower. What feature is this?
hints: It is a drawing with labels.
It shows the parts of a plant.
questions.explanation: A drawing with labels pointing to different parts is a labelled diagram.
questions.misconception: An information text must have pictures.

questions.stem: Which of these features would you NOT expect to find in an information text?
hints: Fairy characters are found in stories.
Information texts are about real things.
questions.explanation: A fairy character is a made-up character, so it does not belong in an information text.
questions.misconception: All texts are stories.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B2.2.7.1: Understand and analyse texts read
indicator.objective: Retell level-appropriate texts in own words

skills.description: Identify the most important events in a text (not every tiny detail).
Retell the text in the correct order (beginning, middle, ending) using own words.
Paraphrase the text rather than copying exact sentences.

misconceptions: Retelling means copying the text.
Every detail must be included.
The order doesn't matter.
A retelling is just a summary.
If you forget a part, you can skip it.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi woke up, ate breakfast, and went to school.' What is the most important event?
hints: What is the main thing Kofi did?
questions.explanation: Going to school is the main event in the sentence.
questions.misconception: Every detail must be included.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama found a lost puppy. She took it home and fed it.' What is the key event?
questions.explanation: The key event is that Ama found a lost puppy.
questions.misconception: Every detail must be included.

questions.stem: Read: 'The farmer planted seeds. He watered them every day. Soon the plants grew tall.' What is the key event?
hints: What is the result of the story?
questions.explanation: The key event is that the plants grew tall.
questions.misconception: Every detail must be included.

questions.stem: Put these events in order: 1. The girl found a coin. 2. She bought sweets. 3. She went to the shop. What is the correct order?
hints: She must find the coin before spending it.
She must go to the shop before buying.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: find the coin, go to the shop, buy sweets (1, 3, 2).
questions.misconception: The order doesn't matter.

questions.stem: Read: 'The boy woke up. He brushed his teeth. He went to school.' What happened first?
hints: What is the first thing in the text?
questions.explanation: The boy woke up first.
questions.misconception: The order doesn't matter.

questions.stem: Read: 'The sun was hot. The children were thirsty. They drank water.' What happened last?
questions.explanation: The last event is that they drank water.
questions.misconception: The order doesn't matter.

questions.stem: The text says: 'The girl was famished.' Which retelling uses your own words?
questions.explanation: The girl was very hungry' uses your own words to explain 'famished'.
questions.misconception: Retelling means copying the text.

questions.stem: The text says: 'The boy was exhausted after the race.' Which retelling is in your own words?
options: The boy was very tired after the race.
The boy was exhausted after the race.
Exhausted after the race was the boy.
hints: It shows you understand the meaning.
questions.explanation: The boy was very tired after the race' uses your own words to retell the sentence.
questions.misconception: Retelling means copying the text.

questions.stem: Which is the best retelling of this sentence: 'The boy was famished and exhausted after the long journey'?
options: The boy was very hungry and very tired after the long trip.
The boy was famished and exhausted after the long journey.
The long journey made the boy famished.
hints: Which sentence changes all three words?
questions.explanation: The boy was very hungry and very tired after the long trip' uses your own words for all three key words.
questions.misconception: Retelling means copying the text.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B2.2.7.1: Understand and analyse texts read
indicator.objective: Ask and answer factual and inferential questions about level-appropriate texts

skills.description: Answer questions whose answers are directly stated in the text.
Answer questions that require reading between the lines.
Formulate simple factual and inferential questions about a text read.

misconceptions: All answers are in the text word for word.
Inferential questions are just guesses.
Factual questions are harder than inferential questions.
You only need to read the question, not the text.
Asking questions is not part of reading.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi is seven years old. He lives in Accra.' How old is Kofi?
hints: Look for the number in the text.
questions.explanation: The text directly states that Kofi is seven years old.
questions.misconception: All answers are in the text word for word.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama has a red bag. She takes it to school every day.' What colour is Ama's bag?
hints: Find the bag in the text.
questions.explanation: The text says Ama has a red bag.
questions.misconception: All answers are in the text word for word.

questions.stem: Read: 'The cat sat on the mat. The dog slept under the table.' Where did the cat sit?
hints: Find the cat in the text.
questions.explanation: The cat sat on the mat.
questions.misconception: You only need to read the question, not the text.

questions.stem: Read: 'Yaa woke up at 6 o'clock. She brushed her teeth and ate breakfast.' What did Yaa do first?
hints: That is the first thing in the text.
questions.explanation: Yaa woke up first at 6 o'clock.
questions.misconception: Factual questions are harder than inferential questions.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kofi looked at his food and pushed the plate away. He said, "I am not hungry."' How does Kofi feel?
options: He does not want to eat
hints: He said he is not hungry.
questions.explanation: Kofi pushed his plate away and said he is not hungry, so he does not want to eat.
questions.misconception: Inferential questions are just guesses.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama's eyes filled with tears when she saw her broken toy.' How does Ama feel?
hints: Tears usually mean a certain feeling.
questions.explanation: Tears and a broken toy suggest Ama feels sad.
questions.misconception: Inferential questions are just guesses.

questions.stem: Read: 'The clouds were dark and the wind was strong. People began to run indoors.' What is likely about to happen?
questions.explanation: Dark clouds, strong wind, and people running indoors suggest a storm is coming.
questions.misconception: Inferential questions are just guesses.

questions.stem: Read: 'The old man walked slowly with a stick. Children ran to help him cross the road.' What does this tell us about the children?
questions.explanation: The children helped the old man, showing they are kind and respectful.
questions.misconception: Inferential questions are just guesses.

questions.stem: Read: 'The market was busy. People were buying and selling food.' Which is a good factual question to ask about this text?
options: What were people doing at the market?
hints: The answer is in the text.
It asks what people were doing.
questions.explanation: What were people doing at the market?' is a factual question because the answer is directly in the text.
questions.misconception: Asking questions is not part of reading.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama was smiling and clapping her hands.' Which is a good inferential question?
hints: Inferential questions ask about feelings or reasons.
The text says she was smiling and clapping.
questions.explanation: Why was Ama happy?' is inferential because the answer is not directly stated but can be inferred.
questions.misconception: Inferential questions are just guesses.

questions.stem: Read: 'The girl was crying because she lost her money.' Which question is NOT answered in the text?
options: How much money did she lose?
hints: Which question asks for information that is not given?
The text does not say how much.
questions.explanation: The text does not say how much money was lost, so that question is not answered.
questions.misconception: All answers are in the text word for word.

questions.stem: Read: 'The teacher gave the pupils homework. They had to write a story about their family.' What did the pupils have to write about?
questions.explanation: The pupils had to write a story about their family.
questions.misconception: You only need to read the question, not the text.

questions.stem: Read: 'The baby was crying and rubbing her eyes.' What does the baby likely need?
hints: What do babies do when they are tired?
questions.explanation: The baby is likely tired and needs sleep because she is rubbing her eyes.
questions.misconception: Inferential questions are just guesses.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kwame has two sisters and one brother.' How many brothers does Kwame have?
questions.explanation: Kwame has one brother.
questions.misconception: All answers are in the text word for word.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B2.2.7.1: Understand and analyse texts read
indicator.objective: Use illustrations, text clues and context to make predictions during reading

skills.description: Look at pictures and illustrations to guess what a text will be about or what will happen next.
Use the title and headings to make predictions about the content of a text.
Check predictions against the text as they read and adjust when new information appears.

misconceptions: A prediction is a random guess.
Once you predict, you can't change your mind.
Pictures are just decoration.
The title tells you everything.
Predictions must always be correct.

questions.stem: Look at the picture: a girl is holding an umbrella and wearing a raincoat. What do you think the weather is like?
hints: An umbrella and raincoat are used in certain weather.
questions.explanation: The girl has an umbrella and raincoat, so it is likely rainy.
questions.misconception: Pictures are just decoration.

questions.stem: The picture shows children wearing school uniforms and carrying bags. Where are they likely going?
questions.explanation: Uniforms and bags suggest the children are going to school.
questions.misconception: Pictures are just decoration.

questions.stem: A picture shows a boy looking at a broken window with a ball near him. What probably happened?
options: He broke the window with the ball
hints: There is a ball and a broken window.
What do boys do with balls?
questions.explanation: The boy likely broke the window while playing with the ball.
questions.misconception: A prediction is a random guess.

questions.stem: The picture shows a dark sky and people running indoors. What is likely about to happen?
questions.explanation: A dark sky and people running indoors suggest a heavy rainstorm is coming.
questions.misconception: A prediction is a random guess.

questions.stem: Read the title: 'The Hungry Lion'. What do you think the story is about?
hints: What does a hungry animal do?
questions.explanation: The title 'The Hungry Lion' suggests the story is about a lion searching for food.
questions.misconception: The title tells you everything.

questions.stem: The heading says: 'How to Plant a Seed'. What kind of text is this?
questions.explanation: The heading 'How to Plant a Seed' tells us it is an information text with instructions.
questions.misconception: The title tells you everything.

questions.stem: Title: 'The Lost Goat'. Which question might the story answer?
hints: What happens to a lost animal?
questions.explanation: The story is about a lost goat, so it will likely answer who found it.
questions.misconception: A prediction is a random guess.

questions.stem: You predicted it would rain today. You look outside and see people carrying umbrellas. What should you do?
hints: Your prediction matches what you see.
questions.explanation: The umbrellas confirm that it is raining, so you keep your prediction.
questions.misconception: Once you predict, you can't change your mind.

questions.stem: You predicted the boy would eat the mango. Then you read: 'The boy gave the mango to his sister.' What should you do?
hints: The text says he gave it away.
questions.explanation: The text shows the boy did not eat the mango, so you should change your prediction.
questions.misconception: Once you predict, you can't change your mind.

questions.stem: While reading, you predicted the ending would be sad. The last sentence says, 'They all lived happily ever after.' What do you do?
options: Adjust your prediction because the ending is happy
Keep your prediction because you like sad endings
hints: Your prediction does not match the text.
questions.explanation: You should adjust your prediction to a happy ending to match the text.
questions.misconception: Once you predict, you can't change your mind.

questions.stem: A picture shows a farmer with a hoe in a field. What is he likely doing?
questions.explanation: The farmer with a hoe in a field is likely farming.
questions.misconception: Pictures are just decoration.

questions.stem: You predicted the story would be about a lion. The title says 'The Lion and the Mouse'. Were you correct?
options: Yes, the title mentions a lion
No, the title is about a mouse
No, the title is about a cat
questions.explanation: The title mentions a lion, so your prediction was correct.
questions.misconception: Predictions must always be correct.

questions.stem: Title: 'The Magic Pot'. Which of these is the most reasonable prediction?
hints: The word 'magic' is in the title.
questions.explanation: The title 'The Magic Pot' suggests the pot has special powers.
questions.misconception: A prediction is a random guess.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B2.2.6.1: Understand word meanings and usages
indicator.objective: Use dictionaries and glossaries to clarify meaning of words

skills.description: Recognise how a dictionary or glossary is organised (alphabetical order, guide words at the top of pages).
Use guide words and alphabetical order to find a word in a dictionary or glossary.
Read the definition of a word in a dictionary and use it to understand the word in context.

misconceptions: Guide words are the definitions.
You can find a word by opening the dictionary anywhere.
A dictionary only has long or difficult words.
The first meaning in the dictionary is always the right one.
Glossaries and dictionaries are the same thing.

questions.stem: How are words arranged in a dictionary?
hints: It starts with A and ends with Z.
Words are organised by their first letter.
questions.explanation: Words in a dictionary are arranged in alphabetical order.
questions.misconception: You can find a word by opening the dictionary anywhere.

questions.stem: What are the words at the top of a dictionary page called?
hints: They show the first and last word on the page.
questions.explanation: The words at the top of a dictionary page are called guide words.
questions.misconception: Guide words are the definitions.

questions.stem: Which word would come FIRST in a dictionary?
questions.explanation: Apple comes first because it starts with 'A', the first letter of the alphabet.
questions.misconception: You can find a word by opening the dictionary anywhere.

questions.stem: The guide words on a page are 'cat' and 'dog'. Which word would you find on this page?
hints: The word must come between 'cat' and 'dog'.
questions.explanation: Cup comes between 'cat' and 'dog' alphabetically, so it would be on this page.
questions.misconception: Guide words are the definitions.

questions.stem: You want to find the word 'mango'. Which guide word page would you look on?
questions.explanation: Mango would be found on a page with guide words like 'man' and 'map'.
questions.misconception: You can find a word by opening the dictionary anywhere.

questions.stem: Which word would you find between the guide words 'sun' and 'tree'?
questions.explanation: Table comes between 'sun' and 'tree' alphabetically.
questions.misconception: Guide words are the definitions.

questions.stem: You are looking for the word 'kite'. Which guide words would help you find it?
questions.explanation: Kite would be found on a page with guide words like 'king' and 'knee'.
questions.misconception: You can find a word by opening the dictionary anywhere.

questions.stem: The guide words are 'chair' and 'chalk'. Which word would NOT be on this page?
questions.explanation: Cheese comes after 'chalk', so it would not be on this page.
questions.misconception: Guide words are the definitions.

questions.stem: A dictionary entry says: 'cat (n): a small furry animal that says meow.' What does 'cat' mean?
hints: Read the definition after the word.
questions.explanation: The dictionary says 'cat' means a small furry animal.
questions.misconception: A dictionary only has long or difficult words.

questions.stem: A dictionary entry says: 'bat (n): 1. a small animal that flies at night. 2. a wooden stick used in sports.' Which meaning fits this sentence: 'The boy hit the ball with a bat'?
hints: What is used to hit a ball?
questions.explanation: The sentence is about sports, so 'bat' means the wooden stick (meaning 2).
questions.misconception: The first meaning in the dictionary is always the right one.

questions.stem: A dictionary entry says: 'bank (n): 1. a place where money is kept. 2. the land at the side of a river.' Which meaning fits: 'We had a picnic on the river bank'?
hints: It is about land near water.
questions.explanation: The sentence is about a river, so 'bank' means the land at the side of a river (meaning 2).
questions.misconception: The first meaning in the dictionary is always the right one.

questions.stem: A dictionary entry says: 'light (n): brightness. (adj): not heavy.' Which meaning fits: 'The light from the sun is bright'?
hints: The sentence talks about the sun.
questions.explanation: The sentence is about brightness, so 'light' is used as a noun meaning brightness.
questions.misconception: The first meaning in the dictionary is always the right one.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B2.2.6.1: Understand word meanings and usages
indicator.objective: Show awareness that homonyms have different meanings in different contexts

skills.description: Recognise words that have the same spelling or pronunciation but different meanings.
Match a homonym to its correct meaning based on the sentence context.
Use homonyms correctly in sentences that show their different meanings.

misconceptions: A word always has the same meaning.
Homonyms are spelled differently.
You can use any meaning of a homonym in any sentence.
Homonyms only exist in English.
If a word looks the same, it means the same.

questions.stem: Which word can mean both an animal and a sports object?
hints: One is an animal that flies at night.
The other is used in cricket.
questions.explanation: Bat is a homonym: it can mean a flying animal or a piece of sports equipment.
questions.misconception: A word always has the same meaning.

questions.stem: Which word can mean a part of a tree and the outer part of your hand?
hints: Dogs make a sound with one meaning.
questions.explanation: Bark is a homonym: it can mean the outer covering of a tree or the sound a dog makes.
questions.misconception: A word always has the same meaning.

questions.stem: Which word can mean a place to keep money and the side of a river?
questions.explanation: Bank is a homonym: it can mean a financial institution or the side of a river.
questions.misconception: If a word looks the same, it means the same.

questions.stem: Which word can mean a circular object and a sound a phone makes?
hints: You wear one on your finger.
questions.explanation: Ring is a homonym: it can mean a circular object worn on a finger or the sound a phone makes.
questions.misconception: A word always has the same meaning.

questions.stem: How can you tell which meaning of 'bat' is being used in a sentence?
options: By looking at the other words in the sentence
hints: Look at the words around it.
questions.explanation: The context of the sentence (the other words) tells you which meaning of 'bat' is being used.
questions.misconception: You can use any meaning of a homonym in any sentence.

questions.stem: Read: 'I saw a bat fly this morning.' What does 'bat' mean here?
questions.explanation: In this sentence, 'bat' means an animal because it can fly.
questions.misconception: You can use any meaning of a homonym in any sentence.

questions.stem: Read: 'My mother bought a tennis bat for me.' What does 'bat' mean here?
hints: You use it to hit a ball.
questions.explanation: In this sentence, 'bat' means a sports object used in tennis.
questions.misconception: You can use any meaning of a homonym in any sentence.

questions.stem: Read: 'The dog's bark was very loud.' What does 'bark' mean here?
questions.explanation: In this sentence, 'bark' means the sound a dog makes.
questions.misconception: If a word looks the same, it means the same.

questions.stem: Read: 'I went to the bank to save my money.' What does 'bank' mean here?
hints: What do you do with money?
questions.explanation: In this sentence, 'bank' means a place to keep money.
questions.misconception: A word always has the same meaning.

questions.stem: Read: 'You are right.' What does 'right' mean here?
hints: It means someone is not wrong.
It is an answer to a question.
questions.explanation: In this sentence, 'right' means correct.

skills.description: Recognise common prefixes and suffixes attached to root words.

questions.stem: What is the prefix in the word 'unhappy'?

questions.stem: What is the suffix in the word 'slowly'?

questions.stem: Which of these is a compound word?
hints: It is made of two smaller words.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a compound word?
