questions.explanation: Your classmates are your audience when you present in front of the class.
questions.misconception: The audience doesn't matter.

questions.stem: Who is the audience if you are showing a picture to your best friend?
questions.explanation: Your best friend is your audience because you are presenting to them.
questions.misconception: The audience doesn't matter.

questions.stem: How might you change how you speak if your audience is a group of small children?
options: Use simpler words and a gentle voice
hints: Small children may not understand big words.
Think about how you talk to a baby.
questions.explanation: When speaking to small children, it is best to use simpler words and a gentle voice so they can understand.
questions.misconception: The audience doesn't matter.

questions.stem: What should you do before giving a presentation?
hints: You need to know what to talk about.
Think about it ahead of time.
questions.explanation: Planning what you will say helps you give a better presentation.
questions.misconception: You don't need to prepare; you can just talk.

questions.stem: Which is a good topic for a short presentation about yourself?
questions.explanation: My favourite food' is a good topic for a short presentation about yourself.
questions.misconception: Only 'big' topics are suitable for presentation.

questions.stem: You have three ideas for your presentation: 1) My name, 2) My favourite game, 3) My school. What is the best order?
options: My name, My school, My favourite game
My school, My name, My favourite game
My favourite game, My name, My school
My name, My favourite game, My school
hints: It is polite to introduce yourself first.
Talk about your game after you say who you are.
questions.explanation: The best order is to introduce yourself first (My name), then talk about something you enjoy (My favourite game), and finally where you go (My school).
questions.misconception: You don't need to prepare; you can just talk.

questions.stem: What does it look like to speak with confidence?
options: Standing up straight and speaking clearly
Looking at the floor and whispering
hints: It shows you are ready to speak.
Your voice is loud enough to hear.
questions.explanation: Standing up straight and speaking clearly are signs of confidence.
questions.misconception: Speaking confidently means speaking loudly.

questions.stem: If you feel shy before presenting, what is a good thing to do?
options: Take a deep breath and try your best
questions.explanation: Taking a deep breath and doing your best helps you build confidence.
questions.misconception: Shy pupils cannot present.

questions.stem: Why should you try to speak clearly and not mumble?
options: So the audience can understand you
So you don't have to speak
So the teacher doesn't hear you
hints: The audience needs to hear your words.
If you mumble, they won't understand.
questions.explanation: Speaking clearly helps the audience understand what you are saying.
questions.misconception: Speaking confidently means speaking loudly.

questions.stem: After your presentation, someone asks you a question. What should you do?
options: Listen and try to answer politely
questions.explanation: Listening and answering politely shows good manners and helps your audience learn more.
questions.misconception: Asking questions after a presentation is rude.

questions.stem: What should you do if someone asks a question and you don't know the answer?
options: Say 'I'm sorry, I don't know' politely
hints: It is okay not to know everything.
questions.explanation: Politely admitting you don't know is better than making up an answer.
questions.misconception: Asking questions after a presentation is rude.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: 9. Giving and Responding to Commands/Instructions/Directions and Making Requests
indicator.content_standard: B2.1.9.1: Demonstrate understanding in commands, instructions, directions and requests
indicator.objective: Make and respond to polite requests

skills.description: Recognise polite request phrases (e.g., 'Please', 'Could you...', 'May I...', 'Do you mind...') and distinguish them from commands.
Make polite requests using appropriate phrases in given situations.
Respond appropriately to polite requests (e.g., 'Yes, of course', 'Sure', 'I'm sorry, I can't').
Explain why using 'please' and polite language matters when making requests.

misconceptions: A command with 'please' is a polite request.
You must always say 'yes' to a request.
Only 'please' makes a request polite.
Requests and commands are the same.
A polite request needs no response.

questions.stem: Which of these is a polite request?
questions.explanation: May I use your pen?' is a polite request because it asks nicely.
questions.misconception: Requests and commands are the same.

questions.stem: Which word in 'Could you please help me?' makes it polite?
hints: It is a word used to ask nicely.
questions.explanation: The word 'Could' makes the request polite because it is a gentle way to ask.
questions.misconception: Only 'please' makes a request polite.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a polite request?
options: Do you mind passing the book?
hints: Look for the sentence that sounds like an order.
questions.explanation: Bring me that book!' is a command, not a polite request, because it is an order without polite words.
questions.misconception: Requests and commands are the same.

questions.stem: Which is a polite way to ask for water?
options: May I have some water, please?
hints: It is a complete, polite sentence.
questions.explanation: May I have some water, please?' is polite because it asks nicely and uses 'please'.
questions.misconception: Only 'please' makes a request polite.

questions.stem: A pupil says to the teacher, 'Do you mind if I open the window?' What type of sentence is this?
hints: The pupil is asking for permission.
They used 'Do you mind', which is very polite.
questions.explanation: This is a polite request because the pupil is asking for permission in a very polite way.
questions.misconception: Requests and commands are the same.

questions.stem: A friend says, 'Can I borrow your eraser?' What should you say?
options: No, I am not your friend
questions.explanation: Yes, of course' is a polite and appropriate response to a polite request.
questions.misconception: You must always say 'yes' to a request.

questions.stem: Your teacher says, 'Could you please close the door?' What is the best response?
options: Yes, teacher. I will close it now
questions.explanation: Yes, teacher. I will close it now' is a polite and respectful response to a polite request.
questions.misconception: A polite request needs no response.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: 9. Giving and Responding to Commands/Instructions/Directions and Making Requests
indicator.content_standard: B2.1.9.1: Demonstrate understanding in commands, instructions, directions and requests
indicator.objective: Give and respond to commands

skills.description: Recognise command sentences (imperatives) such as 'Stand up', 'Close the door', 'Bring your books' and distinguish them from statements or questions.
Respond correctly to simple commands given orally (e.g., stand up, sit down, open your book).
Give clear, polite commands to peers or group members in a role-play or classroom situation.

misconceptions: A command is the same as a question.
Commands must be rude.
Only teachers can give commands.
Any response is fine as long as you do something.
Commands are only spoken, not written.

questions.stem: Which of these is a command?
hints: A command tells someone to do something.
It starts with an action word.
questions.explanation: Close the door' is a command because it tells someone to do something.
questions.misconception: A command is the same as a question.

questions.stem: Which sentence tells someone to do something?
hints: It is an order or instruction.
questions.explanation: Sit down' is a command that tells a person to take a seat.
questions.misconception: Commands must be rude.

questions.stem: Which of these is a polite command?
hints: It is still a command but said nicely.
questions.explanation: Please bring your book' is a polite command because it tells someone to do something but uses the polite word 'please'.
questions.misconception: Commands must be rude.

questions.stem: Which of these signs is a written command?
hints: Signs often tell you what to do.
It starts with an action word.
questions.explanation: Keep off the grass' is a written command found on signs to tell people what to do.
questions.misconception: Commands are only spoken, not written.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a command?
options: I am going to the market.
hints: Look for the sentence that just tells a fact.
The other three tell someone to do something.
questions.explanation: I am going to the market' is a statement, not a command, because it tells a fact rather than telling someone to do something.
questions.misconception: A command is the same as a question.

questions.stem: Your teacher says, 'Open your books.' What should you do?
questions.explanation: You should open your book because the teacher gave the command 'Open your books'.
questions.misconception: Any response is fine as long as you do something.

questions.stem: A friend says, 'Please pass the salt.' What is the correct response?
options: Pass the salt to your friend
hints: Your friend is asking for something.
questions.explanation: You should pass the salt because your friend gave a polite command requesting it.
questions.misconception: Any response is fine as long as you do something.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B2.1.8.1: Demonstrate understanding in asking and answering questions
indicator.objective: Use appropriate pronunciation and intonation in asking and answering Wh – questions

skills.description: Recognise and name the Wh- question words (who, what, where, when, why, how) and what kind of answer each expects.
Ask correct Wh- questions using appropriate pronunciation and falling intonation.
Answer Wh- questions correctly and with appropriate falling intonation.
Match a Wh- question to its correct answer based on meaning.

misconceptions: All Wh- words can be used interchangeably.
Wh- questions use rising intonation.
A one-word answer is always enough.
The question word doesn't change the answer.
Pronunciation doesn't matter in questions.
Any answer is correct if it makes sense.

questions.stem: Which word asks about a person?
questions.explanation: 'Who' is the Wh- word used to ask about a person.
questions.misconception: All Wh- words can be used interchangeably.

questions.stem: Which word asks about a place?
hints: It is used for a location.
questions.explanation: 'Where' is the Wh- word used to ask about a place.
questions.misconception: All Wh- words can be used interchangeably.

questions.stem: Which Wh- word would you use to ask about the time something happened?
questions.explanation: 'When' is used to ask about time.
questions.misconception: All Wh- words can be used interchangeably.

questions.stem: Which Wh- word asks for a reason?
questions.explanation: 'Why' asks for a reason or explanation.
questions.misconception: All Wh- words can be used interchangeably.

questions.stem: You want to know the way someone is feeling. Which Wh- word do you use?
hints: It asks about manner or condition.
questions.explanation: 'How' is used to ask about the way someone feels or the manner of something.
questions.misconception: All Wh- words can be used interchangeably.

questions.stem: Question: 'Who is your teacher?' Which is the best answer?
hints: The question asks about a person.
questions.explanation: 'Who' asks about a person, so 'Mr. Mensah' is the correct answer.
questions.misconception: The question word doesn't change the answer.

questions.stem: Question: 'Where is the library?' Which is the best answer?
hints: The question asks about a place.
questions.explanation: 'Where' asks about a place, so 'Next to the classroom' is correct.
questions.misconception: The question word doesn't change the answer.

questions.stem: Match the question to the answer: 'What is your name?'
hints: The question asks for a name.
questions.explanation: The answer to 'What is your name?' is a name.
questions.misconception: Any answer is correct if it makes sense.

questions.stem: Match the question to the answer: 'How old are you?'
hints: The question asks for an age.
questions.explanation: The answer to 'How old are you?' is an age, like 'I am seven.'
questions.misconception: Any answer is correct if it makes sense.

questions.stem: Match the question to the answer: 'Where do you live?'
hints: The question asks for a place.
questions.explanation: The answer to 'Where do you live?' is a place, like 'In Kumasi.'
questions.misconception: Any answer is correct if it makes sense.

questions.stem: Match the question to the answer: 'Why are you late?'
hints: The question asks for a reason.
questions.explanation: The answer to 'Why are you late?' gives a reason, like 'Because I missed the bus.'
questions.misconception: Any answer is correct if it makes sense.

questions.stem: Match the question to the answer: 'When is your birthday?'
hints: The question asks for a date or time.
questions.explanation: The answer to 'When is your birthday?' is a date, like 'On 5th June.'
questions.misconception: Any answer is correct if it makes sense.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B2.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Recognise and discuss events in a story (characters, settings, moral, etc.)

skills.description: Recognise characters, setting and main events in a story heard.
Talk about what happened in the story and why.
State the moral lesson or value in the story.

misconceptions: Setting is just 'where' and nothing else.
The moral is the same as the story.
Only the main character matters.
Events are not connected.
A story has only one event.

questions.stem: In a story, what do we call the people or animals who take part in the action?
questions.explanation: Characters are the people or animals in a story.
questions.misconception: Only the main character matters.

questions.stem: In a story, what is the setting?
options: Where and when the story happens
hints: It is the background of the story.
questions.explanation: The setting tells us where and when the story takes place.
questions.misconception: Setting is just 'where' and nothing else.

questions.stem: A story says: 'In the village of Techiman, a little girl found a magic ring.' What is the setting of this story?
hints: Look for the name of a place.
questions.explanation: The setting is Techiman, the village where the story takes place.
questions.misconception: Setting is just 'where' and nothing else.

questions.stem: Who is usually the main character in a story?
options: The person or animal the story is mostly about
The person who tells the story
hints: Who does the story focus on?
questions.explanation: The main character is the central person or animal the story is about.
questions.misconception: Only the main character matters.

questions.stem: A story says: 'Kofi was hungry. He ate his food.' What event happened?
questions.explanation: The event is that Kofi ate his food because he was hungry.
questions.misconception: A story has only one event.

questions.stem: A story says: 'Ama found a small bird with a hurt wing. She took it home and bandaged it.' Why did Ama take the bird home?
options: Because she wanted to eat it
hints: What was wrong with the bird?
questions.explanation: Ama took the bird home because it was hurt and needed help.
questions.misconception: Events are not connected.

questions.stem: A story says: 'The boy forgot his umbrella. It rained heavily. He got wet.' What is the cause of the boy getting wet?
options: He forgot his umbrella and it rained
hints: The rain caused him to get wet.
questions.explanation: The boy got wet because he forgot his umbrella and it rained heavily.
questions.misconception: Events are not connected.

questions.stem: A story says: 'The children laughed at the new boy. He felt sad and sat alone.' What does this tell you about the children's behaviour?
hints: How did the new boy feel?
Laughing at someone is not nice.
questions.explanation: Laughing at the new boy made him feel sad, so the behaviour was unkind.
questions.misconception: The moral is the same as the story.

questions.stem: A story says: 'Always tell the truth.' What is the moral of the story?
hints: It is the opposite of lying.
questions.explanation: The moral is to be honest and always tell the truth.
questions.misconception: The moral is the same as the story.

questions.stem: A story is about a lazy ant who has no food in the rainy season. What is the moral?
hints: What happened because the ant was lazy?
The lesson is about working hard.
questions.explanation: The story teaches the importance of hard work and preparing for the future.
questions.misconception: The moral is the same as the story.

questions.stem: A story says: 'The proud lion laughed at the weak mouse. Later, the mouse helped the lion escape a trap.' What is the moral?
options: Even the small can help the great
hints: Who helped who in the end?
The mouse was small but helpful.
questions.explanation: The story teaches that even small or weak creatures can help the great and strong.
questions.misconception: The moral is the same as the story.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B2.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events (beginning, middle and end) in drama

skills.description: Recognise the beginning, middle and ending of a drama heard.
Put events from a drama in the correct order.
Explain why the order of events matters in a drama.

misconceptions: The ending is just the last line spoken.
Any order is fine as long as you tell the events.
The middle is not important.
Drama is the same as a story.
Sequence means just first and last.

questions.stem: In a drama, what happens at the beginning?
options: We meet the characters and learn the problem
hints: It is the first part of the play.
We learn who is in the play.
questions.explanation: The beginning of a drama introduces the characters and the problem they will face.
questions.misconception: The ending is just the last line spoken.

questions.stem: In a drama, what usually happens at the ending?
questions.explanation: The ending of a drama is where the problem is resolved.
questions.misconception: The ending is just the last line spoken.

questions.stem: A drama shows a girl losing her bag, looking for it, and finally finding it. What part is 'looking for it'?
hints: It happens after she loses it.
It happens before she finds it.
questions.explanation: Looking for the bag is the middle part, the main action between the problem and the solution.
questions.misconception: The middle is not important.

questions.stem: In a drama, the actors introduce themselves and their problem. What part of the drama is this?
questions.explanation: Introducing the characters and the problem is the beginning of the drama.
questions.misconception: Sequence means just first and last.

questions.stem: Why is it important for a drama to have a clear beginning, middle, and ending?
options: So the audience can understand the story
So the actors can wear costumes
hints: A clear structure helps them follow the play.
questions.explanation: A clear structure helps the audience follow and understand the story from start to finish.
questions.misconception: Any order is fine as long as you tell the events.

questions.stem: Which event comes first in a drama?
questions.explanation: The actors introducing the problem happens first, at the beginning of the drama.
questions.misconception: Sequence means just first and last.

questions.stem: Put these events in order: Kofi finds a coin, Kofi buys sweets, Kofi loses the coin.
options: Kofi loses the coin, Kofi finds a coin, Kofi buys sweets
Kofi finds a coin, Kofi loses the coin, Kofi buys sweets
Kofi finds a coin, Kofi buys sweets, Kofi loses the coin
Kofi buys sweets, Kofi finds a coin, Kofi loses the coin
hints: He found the coin before losing it.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: Kofi finds the coin, then buys sweets, then loses the coin.
questions.misconception: Any order is fine as long as you tell the events.

questions.stem: In a drama, the actors show a boy planting a seed. Next, they show rain falling. What happens last?
options: The seed grows into a plant
questions.explanation: The last event is the seed growing into a plant after the rain falls.
questions.misconception: Sequence means just first and last.

questions.stem: A drama shows these events: 1. The children clean the classroom. 2. The teacher praises them. 3. The teacher arrives. What is the correct order?
hints: The teacher must arrive before seeing the clean classroom.
questions.explanation: The teacher arrives first (3), then the children clean (1), then the teacher praises them (2).
questions.misconception: Any order is fine as long as you tell the events.

questions.stem: If a drama showed the ending before the beginning, how would the audience feel?
options: Confused and unable to follow the story
hints: The audience needs to see events in order.
questions.explanation: Showing the ending first would confuse the audience because they would not understand how the story led to that point.
questions.misconception: Any order is fine as long as you tell the events.

questions.stem: Why does the order of events matter in a drama?
options: So the story makes sense to the audience
So the actors can remember their lines
hints: If events are mixed up, it's confusing.
questions.explanation: The order of events helps the audience understand how the story unfolds and why things happen.
questions.misconception: Any order is fine as long as you tell the events.

questions.stem: A drama about a hungry dog is told like this: 'The dog found food. The dog was hungry. The dog ate the food.' What is wrong with this order?
options: The dog should be hungry before finding food
The dog should not eat the food
The dog should not be in the drama
The drama should end with the dog being hungry
hints: Does it make sense to find food before being hungry?
The cause comes before the effect.
questions.explanation: The correct order should be: the dog is hungry, then finds food, then eats it.
questions.misconception: Any order is fine as long as you tell the events.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B2.1.6.1: Explore using certain culturally acceptable language for communication
indicator.objective: Use a wide variety of words to talk about manners

skills.description: Recognise and name words related to good manners.
Use polite words appropriately in simple situations.
Explain why good manners are important in the home, school, and community.

misconceptions: Only 'please' and 'thank you' are polite words.
Manners are only for adults.
Manners are only about words.
Using polite words is old-fashioned.

questions.stem: Which of these is a polite word?
hints: You say it when asking for something.
questions.explanation: 'Please' is a polite word used when making a request.
questions.misconception: Only 'please' and 'thank you' are polite words.

questions.stem: What do you say when someone gives you a gift?
questions.explanation: 'Thank you' is said to show gratitude when receiving something.
questions.misconception: Only 'please' and 'thank you' are polite words.

questions.stem: Which word do you use when you accidentally bump into someone?
hints: You did something wrong by accident.
questions.explanation: 'Sorry' is used to apologise when you have made a mistake or hurt someone.
questions.misconception: Only 'please' and 'thank you' are polite words.

questions.stem: Which word do you use to get someone's attention politely?
hints: It is a polite way to interrupt.
questions.explanation: 'Excuse me' is a polite way to get someone's attention or interrupt them.
questions.misconception: Only 'please' and 'thank you' are polite words.

questions.stem: You want to borrow a pencil from a friend. What should you say?
options: May I borrow your pencil, please?
questions.explanation: Asking politely with 'May I... please?' shows good manners when borrowing something.
questions.misconception: Using polite words is old-fashioned.

questions.stem: Your teacher helps you with your work. What should you say?
questions.explanation: Saying 'Thank you' shows gratitude when someone helps you.
questions.misconception: Manners are only for adults.

questions.stem: Why is it important to say 'please' and 'thank you'?
options: It shows respect and makes people happy to help
It is a rule in school only
hints: How do you feel when someone thanks you?
questions.explanation: Using polite words shows respect and makes people feel appreciated.
questions.misconception: Using polite words is old-fashioned.

questions.stem: Two pupils want the same book. One says 'Give me the book!' and the other says 'May I have the book, please?' Who shows good manners?
questions.explanation: The second pupil shows good manners by asking politely with 'May I... please?'.
questions.misconception: Using polite words is old-fashioned.

questions.stem: A new pupil joins your class. How can you use good manners to make them feel welcome?
hints: Think about how you would feel in a new class.
questions.explanation: Welcoming a new pupil politely helps them feel accepted and comfortable.
questions.misconception: Manners are only about words.
